The exegesis of the Almighty's words: ﴿By the sky and the Night-Comer. And what will make you know what the Night-Comer is? It is the piercing star. There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian. So let man consider from what he was created. He was created from a gushing fluid, that issues from between the loins and the ribs. Indeed, He is able to return him. On the Day when secrets are examined. Then he will have no power nor any helper.﴾

Our Lord swore by the sky and by the *ṭāriq*, the one who comes at night, from among the bright stars, which are hidden by day. Whatever comes at night has "knocked" (*ṭaraqa*).

Something similar to what we have said on this was said by the people of *ta'wīl* (the interpreters of the Qur'an).

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbās, regarding ﴿By the sky and the Night-Comer﴾: "The sky and what comes to it at night."

﴿And what will make you know what the Night-Comer is?﴾ Almighty God says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): "And what made you aware, O Muhammad, of what the Night-Comer is, by which I have sworn? On His words: ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian﴾

The readers (*qurrā'*, the transmitters of the Qur'anic recitation variants) differed in reading this. Among the readers of Medina, Abū Ja'far read it, and among the readers of Kufa, Ḥamzah read ﴿*lammā* 'alayhā﴾ with a doubled *mīm* (lamma, with shadda). It is also reported from al-Ḥasan that he read it that way.

- Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf related to me, saying: Abū 'Ubayd related to us, saying: Ḥajjāj related to us, from Hārūn, from al-Ḥasan, that he used to recite it ﴿inna kullu nafsin lammā 'alayhā ḥāfiẓ﴾ with the doubled *mīm*, and he would say: "*illā* 'alayhā ḥāfiẓ" (except that over it there is a guardian). And so every instance in the Qur'an is recited with the doubled form.

Nāfi' of Medina read it, and Abū 'Amr of Basra, with the single *mīm*: ﴿*lamā*﴾, meaning: "Indeed every soul has over it a guardian," with the *lām* being the answer to *inna* ("indeed"), and the *mā* following it being an extra particle. In that case there is no doubling.

The reading which I do not choose other than is the single form, because that is the familiar speech of the Arabs. Some scholars of Arabic speech have rejected the doubled form, holding that it is not known in Arabic usage. Al-Farrā' used to say: "We do not know the basis for the doubled reading, and we think it is a dialect of the Hudhayl tribe, who use *illā* together with the lightened *inna*, as *lammā*, and go no further than that, as if he said: 'Every soul has over it only a guardian.'" If what al-Farrā' mentioned is correct, that it is the dialect of Hudhayl, then reciting by it is permissible and sound. But the preferred choice, once that is established with us, is the other reading, the single form, because it is the familiar speech of the Arabs, and the more familiar should not be abandoned for the less familiar.

- Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf has related to me, saying: Abū 'Ubayd related to us, saying: Mu'ādh related to us, from Ibn 'Awn, who said: "I recited before Ibn Sīrīn, ﴿inna kullu nafsin lammā 'alayhā ḥāfiẓ﴾, and he rejected it and said: 'Glory be to God, glory be to God!'"

So the meaning of the statement is: "Indeed every soul has over it a guardian from its Lord, who watches its deeds and counts what it earns of good or evil."

Something similar to what we have said on this was said by the people of *ta'wīl*.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbās, his word ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian﴾: "Every soul has over it guardians from among the angels."
- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazīd related to us, saying: Sa'īd related to us, from Qatādah, his word: "Guardians who watch your deeds, your provision and your term. When you complete it, O son of Adam, you are taken up to your Lord."

* *

On His words: ﴿So let man consider from what he was created﴾

Almighty God says: So let man, who denies resurrection after death and rejects God's power to bring him back to life after his death, consider ﴿from what he was created﴾, that is: from what thing his Lord created him. Then He, glory be to Him, informed about what He created him from, saying: ﴿He was created from a gushing fluid﴾, meaning: from a poured-out water. This is the form *dāfiq* (active participle) used with the sense of *madfūq* (passive), which the Arabs employ, and it is said that most of the Arab tribes who use it are the inhabitants of the Ḥijāz, when it is in the manner of an adjective, as in their saying: *hādhā sirrun kātim* (this is a hidden secret) and *hammun nāṣib* (a standing worry), and the like.

The most correct of these views, in our judgment, is the view of those who said: the meaning is: indeed God is able to return man, who was created from a gushing water, after his death, alive, in the form he had before his death.

On His words: ﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾

Almighty God says: Indeed, this One who created you, O people, from this gushing water, and made you a complete human being after you were a poured-out water, is able to return you.

The people of *ta'wīl* differed over the pronoun in His words ﴿'alā rajʿihi﴾ (to return him), as to what it refers back to. Some of them said: it refers back to the water. They said: the meaning of the sentence is: indeed God is able to return the drop to the place from which it came out.

On His words: ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian﴾

The readers (*qurrā'*, the transmitters of the Qur'anic recitation variants) differed in reading this. Among the readers of Medina, Abū Ja'far read it, and among the readers of Kufa, Ḥamzah read ﴿*lammā* 'alayhā﴾ with a doubled *mīm* (lamma, with shadda). It is also reported from al-Ḥasan that he read it that way.

- Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf related to me, saying: Abū 'Ubayd related to us, saying: Ḥajjāj related to us, from Hārūn, from al-Ḥasan, that he used to recite it ﴿inna kullu nafsin lammā 'alayhā ḥāfiẓ﴾ with the doubled *mīm*, and he would say: "*illā* 'alayhā ḥāfiẓ" (except that over it there is a guardian). And so every instance in the Qur'an is recited with the doubled form.

Nāfi' of Medina read it, and Abū 'Amr of Basra, with the single *mīm*: ﴿*lamā*﴾, meaning: "Indeed every soul has over it a guardian," with the *lām* being the answer to *inna* ("indeed"), and the *mā* following it being an extra particle. In that case there is no doubling.

The reading which I do not choose other than is the single form, because that is the familiar speech of the Arabs. Some scholars of Arabic speech have rejected the doubled form, holding that it is not known in Arabic usage. Al-Farrā' used to say: "We do not know the basis for the doubled reading, and we think it is a dialect of the Hudhayl tribe, who use *illā* together with the lightened *inna*, as *lammā*, and go no further than that, as if he said: 'Every soul has over it only a guardian.'" If what al-Farrā' mentioned is correct, that it is the dialect of Hudhayl, then reciting by it is permissible and sound. But the preferred choice, once that is established with us, is the other reading, the single form, because it is the familiar speech of the Arabs, and the more familiar should not be abandoned for the less familiar.

- Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf has related to me, saying: Abū 'Ubayd related to us, saying: Mu'ādh related to us, from Ibn 'Awn, who said: "I recited before Ibn Sīrīn, ﴿inna kullu nafsin lammā 'alayhā ḥāfiẓ﴾, and he rejected it and said: 'Glory be to God, glory be to God!'"

So the meaning of the statement is: "Indeed every soul has over it a guardian from its Lord, who watches its deeds and counts what it earns of good or evil."

Something similar to what we have said on this was said by the people of *ta'wīl*.

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazīd related to us, saying: Sa'īd related to us, from Qatādah, his word: "Guardians who watch your deeds, your provision and your term. When you complete it, O son of Adam, you are taken up to your Lord."

On His words: ﴿So let man consider from what he was created﴾

Almighty God says: So let man, who denies resurrection after death and rejects God's power to bring him back to life after his death, consider ﴿from what he was created﴾, that is: from what thing his Lord created him. This is the form *dāfiq* (active participle) used with the sense of *madfūq* (passive), which the Arabs employ, and it is said that most of the Arab tribes who use it are the inhabitants of the Ḥijāz, when it is in the manner of an adjective, as in their saying: *hādhā sirrun kātim* (this is a hidden secret) and *hammun nāṣib* (a standing worry), and the like.

On His words: ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian﴾

The readers (*qurrā'*, the transmitters of the Qur'anic recitation variants) differed in reading this. Among the readers of Medina, Abū Ja'far read it, and among the readers of Kufa, Ḥamzah read ﴿*lammā* 'alayhā﴾ with a doubled *mīm* (lamma, with shadda). It is also reported from al-Ḥasan that he read it that way.

- Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf related to me, saying: Abū 'Ubayd related to us, saying: Ḥajjāj related to us, from Hārūn, from al-Ḥasan, that he used to recite it ﴿inna kullu nafsin lammā 'alayhā ḥāfiẓ﴾ with the doubled *mīm*, and he would say: "*illā* 'alayhā ḥāfiẓ" (except that over it there is a guardian). And so every instance in the Qur'an is recited with the doubled form.

Nāfi' of Medina read it, and Abū 'Amr of Basra, with the single *mīm*: ﴿*lamā*﴾, meaning: "Indeed every soul has over it a guardian," with the *lām* being the answer to *inna* ("indeed"), and the *mā* following it being an extra particle. In that case there is no doubling.

The reading which I do not choose other than is the single form, because that is the familiar speech of the Arabs. Some scholars of Arabic speech have rejected the doubled form, holding that it is not known in Arabic usage. Al-Farrā' used to say: "We do not know the basis for the doubled reading, and we think it is a dialect of the Hudhayl tribe, who use *illā* together with the lightened *inna*, as *lammā*, and go no further than that, as if he said: 'Every soul has over it only a guardian.'" If what al-Farrā' mentioned is correct, that it is the dialect of Hudhayl, then reciting by it is permissible and sound. But the preferred choice, once that is established with us, is the other reading, the single form, because it is the familiar speech of the Arabs, and the more familiar should not be abandoned for the less familiar.

- Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf has related to me, saying: Abū 'Ubayd related to us, saying: Mu'ādh related to us, from Ibn 'Awn, who said: "I recited before Ibn Sīrīn, ﴿inna kullu nafsin lammā 'alayhā ḥāfiẓ﴾, and he rejected it and said: 'Glory be to God, glory be to God!'"

So the meaning of the statement is: "Indeed every soul has over it a guardian from its Lord, who watches its deeds and counts what it earns of good or evil."

On His words: ﴿So let man consider from what he was created﴾

Almighty God says: So let man, who denies resurrection after death and rejects God's power to bring him back to life after his death, consider ﴿from what he was created﴾, that is: from what thing his Lord created him. On His words: ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian﴾

The readers (*qurrā'*, the transmitters of the Qur'anic recitation variants) differed in reading this. Among the readers of Medina, Abū Ja'far read it, and among the readers of Kufa, Ḥamzah read ﴿*lammā* 'alayhā﴾ with a doubled *mīm* (lamma, with shadda). It is also reported from al-Ḥasan that he read it that way.

- Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf related to me, saying: Abū 'Ubayd related to us, saying: Ḥajjāj related to us, from Hārūn, from al-Ḥasan, that he used to recite it ﴿inna kullu nafsin lammā 'alayhā ḥāfiẓ﴾ with the doubled *mīm*, and he would say: "*illā* 'alayhā ḥāfiẓ" (except that over it there is a guardian). And so every instance in the Qur'an is recited with the doubled form.

Nāfi' of Medina read it, and Abū 'Amr of Basra, with the single *mīm*: ﴿*lamā*﴾, meaning: "Indeed every soul has over it a guardian," with the *lām* being the answer to *inna* ("indeed"), and the *mā* following it being an extra particle. In that case there is no doubling.

The reading which I do not choose other than is the single form, because that is the familiar speech of the Arabs. Some scholars of Arabic speech have rejected the doubled form, holding that it is not known in Arabic usage. Al-Farrā' used to say: "We do not know the basis for the doubled reading, and we think it is a dialect of the Hudhayl tribe, who use *illā* together with the lightened *inna*, as *lammā*, and go no further than that, as if he said: 'Every soul has over it only a guardian.'" If what al-Farrā' mentioned is correct, that it is the dialect of Hudhayl, then reciting by it is permissible and sound. But the preferred choice, once that is established with us, is the other reading, the single form, because it is the familiar speech of the Arabs, and the more familiar should not be abandoned for the less familiar.

- Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf has related to me, saying: Abū 'Ubayd related to us, saying: Mu'ādh related to us, from Ibn 'Awn, who said: "I recited before Ibn Sīrīn, ﴿inna kullu nafsin lammā 'alayhā ḥāfiẓ﴾, and he rejected it and said: 'Glory be to God, glory be to God!'"

So the meaning of the statement is: "Indeed every soul has over it a guardian from its Lord, who watches its deeds and counts what it earns of good or evil."

Almighty God says: So let man, who denies resurrection after death and rejects God's power to bring him back to life after his death, consider ﴿from what he was created﴾, that is: from what thing his Lord created him. I say that this is the most correct view because of His words ﴿On the Day when secrets are examined﴾. The following of His words ﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾ is news of the events of the Resurrection, which indicates that what precedes it is also about that. And ﴿On the Day when secrets are examined﴾ means: He is able to bring him back to life after his death, on the Day when secrets are examined. So "the Day" is a description of the return, because the meaning is: indeed He is able to return him on the Day when secrets are examined.

By His words ﴿On the Day when secrets are examined﴾ is meant: the Day when the secrets of the servants are tested, and what was hidden from the eyes of the servants in the world becomes manifest that Day, namely the obligations which God imposed on him and charged him to carry out.

Something similar to what we have said on this was said by the people of *ta'wīl*.

Mention of those who said that:

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazīd related to us, saying: Sa'īd related to us, from Qatādah, regarding ﴿On the Day when secrets are examined﴾: "These secrets are being tested, so keep good hidden and make it known, if you are able. And there is no power except by God."
- Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, saying: Mihrān related to us, from Sufyān, regarding ﴿On the Day when secrets are examined﴾: "It is tested."

And His saying: ﴿So he will have no power, nor any helper﴾.

He, exalted is His mention, says: So the disbelieving human will have, on that Day, no power by which he can defend himself against the punishment of God and His painful retribution, and no helper to support him and rescue him from the one who has inflicted upon him something hateful. And in the world he used to resort to a power from his tribe, by which he would defend himself against whoever intended him harm, and to a helper from an ally who would support him against the one who wronged and oppressed him.

Those who interpret the Qur'an (ahl al-ta'wil) have said in agreement with what we have said regarding this.

Mention of those who said that:

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿So he will have no power, nor any helper﴾: (no helper) who will support him from God.

On His words: ﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾

Almighty God says: Indeed, this One who created you, O people, from this gushing water, and made you a complete human being after you were a poured-out water, is able to return you.

The people of *ta'wīl* differed over the pronoun in His words ﴿'alā rajʿihi﴾ (to return him), as to what it refers back to. Some of them said: it refers back to the water. They said: the meaning of the sentence is: indeed God is able to return the drop to the place from which it came out.

Mention of those who said that:

- Ibn al-Muthannā related to us, saying: Abū al-Nu'mān al-Ḥakam ibn 'Abd Allāh related to us, saying: Shu'bah related to us, from Abū Rajā', from 'Ikrimah, regarding his word ﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾: "To the loins."
- 'Ubayd ibn Ismā'īl al-Hibārī related to me, saying: 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn Muḥammad al-Muḥāribī related to us, from Layth, from Mujāhid, regarding his word ﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾: "To return the water into the urethra."
- Naṣr ibn 'Abd al-Raḥmān al-Awdī al-Washshā' related to me, saying: Abū Quṭan 'Amr ibn al-Haytham related to us, from Warqā', from 'Abd Allāh ibn Abī Najīḥ, from 'Abd Allāh ibn Abī Bakr, from Mujāhid, regarding his word ﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾: "To return the drop into the urethra."

- Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, saying: Mihrān related to us, from Sufyān, from Layth, from Mujāhid, ﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾: "He returns it into the urethra."

Others said: rather, the meaning is: indeed He is able to return man to water as he was before He created him from it.

- I was told from al-Ḥusayn, who said: I heard Abū Mu'ādh say: 'Ubayd related to us, saying: I heard al-Ḍaḥḥāk say, regarding his word ﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾: "If I wish, I return him as I created him from water."

Others said: rather, the meaning is: indeed He is able to hold back that water.

Mention of those who said that:

Others said: rather, the meaning is that He is able to return man from the state of old age to the state of youth.

Mention of those who said that:

Others, who claimed that the pronoun refers to man, said: the meaning is that He is able to bring him back to life after his death.

I say that this is the most correct view because of His words ﴿On the Day when secrets are examined﴾. The following of His words ﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾ is news of the events of the Resurrection, which indicates that what precedes it is also about that. And ﴿On the Day when secrets are examined﴾ means: He is able to bring him back to life after his death, on the Day when secrets are examined. So "the Day" is a description of the return, because the meaning is: indeed He is able to return him on the Day when secrets are examined.

By His words ﴿On the Day when secrets are examined﴾ is meant: the Day when the secrets of the servants are tested, and what was hidden from the eyes of the servants in the world becomes manifest that Day, namely the obligations which God imposed on him and charged him to carry out.

On His words: ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian﴾

The readers (*qurrā'*, the transmitters of the Qur'anic recitation variants) differed in reading this. Among the readers of Medina, Abū Ja'far read it, and among the readers of Kufa, Ḥamzah read ﴿*lammā* 'alayhā﴾ with a doubled *mīm* (lamma, with shadda). It is also reported from al-Ḥasan that he read it that way.

- Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf related to me, saying: Abū 'Ubayd related to us, saying: Ḥajjāj related to us, from Hārūn, from al-Ḥasan, that he used to recite it ﴿inna kullu nafsin lammā 'alayhā ḥāfiẓ﴾ with the doubled *mīm*, and he would say: "*illā* 'alayhā ḥāfiẓ" (except that over it there is a guardian). And so every instance in the Qur'an is recited with the doubled form.

Nāfi' of Medina read it, and Abū 'Amr of Basra, with the single *mīm*: ﴿*lamā*﴾, meaning: "Indeed every soul has over it a guardian," with the *lām* being the answer to *inna* ("indeed"), and the *mā* following it being an extra particle. In that case there is no doubling.

The reading which I do not choose other than is the single form, because that is the familiar speech of the Arabs. Some scholars of Arabic speech have rejected the doubled form, holding that it is not known in Arabic usage. Al-Farrā' used to say: "We do not know the basis for the doubled reading, and we think it is a dialect of the Hudhayl tribe, who use *illā* together with the lightened *inna*, as *lammā*, and go no further than that, as if he said: 'Every soul has over it only a guardian.'" If what al-Farrā' mentioned is correct, that it is the dialect of Hudhayl, then reciting by it is permissible and sound. But the preferred choice, once that is established with us, is the other reading, the single form, because it is the familiar speech of the Arabs, and the more familiar should not be abandoned for the less familiar.

- Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf has related to me, saying: Abū 'Ubayd related to us, saying: Mu'ādh related to us, from Ibn 'Awn, who said: "I recited before Ibn Sīrīn, ﴿inna kullu nafsin lammā 'alayhā ḥāfiẓ﴾, and he rejected it and said: 'Glory be to God, glory be to God!'"

So the meaning of the statement is: "Indeed every soul has over it a guardian from its Lord, who watches its deeds and counts what it earns of good or evil."

Something similar to what we have said on this was said by the people of *ta'wīl*.

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazīd related to us, saying: Sa'īd related to us, from Qatādah, his word: "Guardians who watch your deeds, your provision and your term. When you complete it, O son of Adam, you are taken up to your Lord."

On His words: ﴿So let man consider from what he was created﴾

Almighty God says: So let man, who denies resurrection after death and rejects God's power to bring him back to life after his death, consider ﴿from what he was created﴾, that is: from what thing his Lord created him. On His words: ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian﴾

The readers (*qurrā'*, the transmitters of the Qur'anic recitation variants) differed in reading this. Among the readers of Medina, Abū Ja'far read it, and among the readers of Kufa, Ḥamzah read ﴿*lammā* 'alayhā﴾ with a doubled *mīm* (lamma, with shadda). It is also reported from al-Ḥasan that he read it that way.

- Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf related to me, saying: Abū 'Ubayd related to us, saying: Ḥajjāj related to us, from Hārūn, from al-Ḥasan, that he used to recite it ﴿inna kullu nafsin lammā 'alayhā ḥāfiẓ﴾ with the doubled *mīm*, and he would say: "*illā* 'alayhā ḥāfiẓ" (except that over it there is a guardian). And so every instance in the Qur'an is recited with the doubled form.

Nāfi' of Medina read it, and Abū 'Amr of Basra, with the single *mīm*: ﴿*lamā*﴾, meaning: "Indeed every soul has over it a guardian," with the *lām* being the answer to *inna* ("indeed"), and the *mā* following it being an extra particle. In that case there is no doubling.

The reading which I do not choose other than is the single form, because that is the familiar speech of the Arabs. Some scholars of Arabic speech have rejected the doubled form, holding that it is not known in Arabic usage. Al-Farrā' used to say: "We do not know the basis for the doubled reading, and we think it is a dialect of the Hudhayl tribe, who use *illā* together with the lightened *inna*, as *lammā*, and go no further than that, as if he said: 'Every soul has over it only a guardian.'" If what al-Farrā' mentioned is correct, that it is the dialect of Hudhayl, then reciting by it is permissible and sound. But the preferred choice, once that is established with us, is the other reading, the single form, because it is the familiar speech of the Arabs, and the more familiar should not be abandoned for the less familiar.

- Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf has related to me, saying: Abū 'Ubayd related to us, saying: Mu'ādh related to us, from Ibn 'Awn, who said: "I recited before Ibn Sīrīn, ﴿inna kullu nafsin lammā 'alayhā ḥāfiẓ﴾, and he rejected it and said: 'Glory be to God, glory be to God!'"

So the meaning of the statement is: "Indeed every soul has over it a guardian from its Lord, who watches its deeds and counts what it earns of good or evil."

Something similar to what we have said on this was said by the people of *ta'wīl*.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbās, his word ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian﴾: "Every soul has over it guardians from among the angels."
- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazīd related to us, saying: Sa'īd related to us, from Qatādah, his word: "Guardians who watch your deeds, your provision and your term. When you complete it, O son of Adam, you are taken up to your Lord."

On His words: ﴿So let man consider from what he was created﴾

Almighty God says: So let man, who denies resurrection after death and rejects God's power to bring him back to life after his death, consider ﴿from what he was created﴾, that is: from what thing his Lord created him. Then He, glory be to Him, informed about what He created him from, saying: ﴿He was created from a gushing fluid﴾, meaning: from a poured-out water. This is the form *dāfiq* (active participle) used with the sense of *madfūq* (passive), which the Arabs employ, and it is said that most of the Arab tribes who use it are the inhabitants of the Ḥijāz, when it is in the manner of an adjective, as in their saying: *hādhā sirrun kātim* (this is a hidden secret) and *hammun nāṣib* (a standing worry), and the like.
